Section: How to use this guide
This guide contains general career-learning guidance. Role expectations vary by employer and location. It does not contain live job listings, salary data, or current hiring requirements. Use it as a starting point and compare its suggestions with recent job descriptions from the places where you plan to apply.

Section: Exploring technology roles
Software developers design, build, test, and maintain software. Common foundations include one programming language, problem-solving, version control with Git, debugging, and basic software design. A small, finished project that is easy to run and explain can help demonstrate practical skills.

Data analysts organize and examine data to answer questions. Useful foundations include spreadsheets, SQL, data cleaning, basic statistics, and communicating results with clear charts or summaries. A portfolio project should explain the question, the data-cleaning choices, and what the results can and cannot show.

Cybersecurity analysts help monitor systems, investigate alerts, and reduce security risks. Useful foundations include networking, operating-system basics, identity and access concepts, security fundamentals, and careful written documentation. Practice in legal labs or systems you own or have permission to use.

Section: Exploring technology roles
Quality assurance testers check whether software behaves as expected and report defects clearly. Useful foundations include test design, careful observation, writing reproducible bug reports, and understanding how users interact with a product. Basic programming and API testing can expand the kinds of testing work you can take on.

Section: A practical learning sequence
Start by reviewing several job descriptions for the role and location you care about. Record repeated skills and separate required skills from preferred ones. This is a research exercise; this app does not fetch job listings for you.

Choose one foundational skill to learn at a time. Alternate short lessons with hands-on practice, and keep brief notes about what worked and what was confusing. Build a small project that uses the skills together, then ask someone to review the instructions and explain what is unclear.

Before applying, make sure your resume describes your contribution accurately. Prepare a short explanation of a project: the problem, your approach, a challenge, and what you would improve next. Do not claim experience, results, or credentials you do not have.

Section: Building a portfolio project
Pick a small problem you understand and define a finish line before you start. Keep the project within the tools and time you have. Include a README with the purpose, setup steps, example use, and known limitations. If you use public data, name the source and check its terms. Avoid publishing private information, API keys, or data you do not have permission to share.

Examples include a simple task-tracking web app for software development, a documented analysis of a public dataset for data analytics, a home-lab security checklist using authorized practice systems for cybersecurity, or a concise test plan with reproducible examples for quality assurance.

Section: Interview practice
For experience questions, organize an honest example around the situation, your responsibility, the actions you took, and the result or lesson. A class assignment, volunteer task, personal project, or part-time job can provide a useful example when you are early in your career. Keep the explanation specific, state your own contribution, and do not invent numbers or outcomes.

For technical questions, explain your assumptions, ask a clarifying question when needed, work through the problem in small steps, and check edge cases. If you do not know something, say what you would investigate and why.

Section: Learning plans
A useful learning plan names a target role, current starting point, available weekly study time, and a time horizon. Reserve time for practice and review, not only lessons. Adjust the plan when a task takes longer than expected. A short plan can build momentum, but it cannot guarantee readiness or employment.

Section: Page 2
Study and Interview Notes  |  Page 2
1. Data Science
Basic Questions
Q1. What is Data Science?
 Ans: An interdisciplinary field that uses statistics, programming, domain knowledge and machine learning to
extract insights and build predictive solutions from structured and unstructured data.
Q2. Explain the Data Science lifecycle.
 Ans: 1) Problem definition 2) Data collection 3) Data cleaning 4) Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) 5) Feature
engineering 6) Model building 7) Evaluation 8) Deployment 9) Monitoring and maintenance.
Q3. Difference between Data Science, Data Analytics and Data Engineering?
 Ans: Data Science: predictive/prescriptive modelling. Data Analytics: descriptive analysis and reporting of
past data. Data Engineering: building pipelines, storage and infrastructure for data.
Q4. Structured vs Unstructured data?
 Ans: Structured: organised in rows/columns (SQL tables, CSV). Unstructured: no fixed schema (text,
images, audio, video). Semi-structured: JSON, XML.
Q5. What is Big Data? Mention the 5 Vs.
 Ans: Datasets too large/complex for traditional tools. Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, Value.
Q6. Population vs Sample?
 Ans: Population is the entire group of

Section: Page 2
interest; a sample is a subset used to draw inferences about the
population.
Q7. Which Python libraries are used in Data Science?
 Ans: NumPy, Pandas, Matplotlib, Seaborn, SciPy, Scikit-learn, Statsmodels, TensorFlow/PyTorch.
Statistics and Data Cleaning
Q8. Mean, Median, Mode - when to use each?
 Ans: Mean for symmetric data, median for skewed data or outliers, mode for categorical data.
Q9. What is standard deviation and variance?
 Ans: Variance is the average squared deviation from the mean; standard deviation is its square root and
shows spread in original units.
Q10. What is a p-value?
 Ans: The probability of observing results at least as extreme as the sample, assuming the null hypothesis is
true. If p < alpha (usually 0.05), reject the null hypothesis.
Q11. Type I vs Type II error?
 Ans: Type I: rejecting a true null (false positive). Type II: failing to reject a false null (false negative).
Q12. What is the Central Limit Theorem?
 Ans: The distribution of sample means approaches a normal distribution as sample size grows (n >= 30 is a
common rule), regardless of the population distribution.
Q13. Correlation vs Causation?
 Ans: Correlation shows two variables move

Section: Page 2
together; causation means one directly causes change in the
other. Correlation does not imply causation.
Q14. How do you handle missing values?
 Ans: Remove rows/columns, impute with mean/median/mode, forward/backward fill, KNN or model-based
imputation, or flag missingness as a feature.
Q15. How do you detect and handle outliers?
 Ans: Detect with IQR rule (below Q1-1.5*IQR or above Q3+1.5*IQR), Z-score (|z|>3), box plots. Handle by
removing, capping (winsorizing), transforming (log) or using robust models.

Section: Page 3
Study and Interview Notes  |  Page 3
Q16. Normalization vs Standardization?
 Ans: Normalization (Min-Max) scales to [0,1]. Standardization (Z-score) gives mean 0 and std 1. Use
standardization for algorithms assuming Gaussian data and distance-based models.
Q17. What is feature engineering?
 Ans: Creating, transforming or selecting variables (e.g., date parts, ratios, encodings, binning) to improve
model performance.
Q18. Label encoding vs One-hot encoding?
 Ans: Label encoding maps categories to integers (suitable for ordinal data). One-hot creates binary columns
per category (suitable for nominal data).
Scenario / Practical Questions
Q19. Your dataset is highly imbalanced (95% / 5%). What will you do?
 Ans: Use resampling (SMOTE oversampling, undersampling), class weights, appropriate metrics (Precision,
Recall, F1, PR-AUC instead of accuracy) and stratified cross-validation.
Q20. How would you explain a model to a non-technical stakeholder?
 Ans: Focus on business impact, use simple visuals, analogies and key drivers (feature importance, SHAP),
avoid jargon, and state limitations.
Q21. How do you perform EDA in Pandas?
 Ans: Check shape, dtypes, missing values, describe(),

Section: Page 3
value_counts(), distributions, correlations and
visualisations.
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('data.csv')
print(df.shape); print(df.info())
print(df.describe()); print(df.isnull().sum())
df = df.fillna(df.median(numeric_only=True))
print(df.corr(numeric_only=True))

Section: Page 4
Study and Interview Notes  |  Page 4
2. Data Analysis using Power BI
Basic Questions
Q22. What is Power BI?
 Ans: Microsoft's business intelligence tool for connecting to data, transforming, modelling and visualising it
through reports and dashboards.
Q23. Main components of Power BI?
 Ans: Power BI Desktop (authoring), Power BI Service (cloud sharing), Power BI Mobile, Power BI Report
Server, Power BI Gateway, Power Query and DAX.
Q24. Report vs Dashboard?
 Ans: A report is multi-page with many visuals built on one dataset. A dashboard is a single-page canvas of
pinned tiles from multiple reports.
Q25. What is Power Query?
 Ans: ETL tool (M language) used to connect, clean, transform and shape data before loading it into the
model.
Q26. What is DAX?
 Ans: Data Analysis Expressions - a formula language for calculated columns, measures and tables.
Q27. Import mode vs DirectQuery vs Live Connection?
 Ans: Import: data cached in memory, fastest. DirectQuery: queries source live, no data stored. Live
Connection: connects to SSAS/Power BI dataset; model lives externally. Composite models mix modes.
Q28. What is a Gateway?
 Ans: A bridge allowing Power BI Service to securely refresh

Section: Page 4
data from on-premises sources. Types:
On-premises (standard) and Personal mode.
Data Modelling and DAX
Q29. What is a Star Schema?
 Ans: A model with a central fact table (transactions) linked to dimension tables (customer, product, date). It is
the recommended modelling pattern for performance and simplicity.
Q30. Types of relationships in Power BI?
 Ans: One-to-many (most common), one-to-one, many-to-many. Cross-filter direction can be single or both.
Q31. Calculated column vs Measure?
 Ans: Calculated column: computed row by row at refresh, stored in memory, usable in slicers/rows. Measure:
computed at query time based on filter context, not stored, used for aggregations.
Q32. What is filter context and row context?
 Ans: Filter context is the set of filters (slicers, rows, columns, CALCULATE) applied to a calculation. Row
context iterates row by row (calculated columns, iterator functions like SUMX).
Q33. Explain CALCULATE().
 Ans: It evaluates an expression in a modified filter context.
Sales India = CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), Sales[Country] = "India")
Q34. SUM vs SUMX?
 Ans: SUM aggregates a single column. SUMX is an iterator that evaluates an expression row by row,

Section: Page 4
then
sums.
Total Revenue = SUMX(Sales, Sales[Qty] * Sales[Price])
Q35. Write a DAX for Year-to-Date and Previous Year sales.
 Ans: Requires a proper Date table marked as Date Table.
YTD Sales = TOTALYTD(SUM(Sales[Amount]), 'Date'[Date])
PY Sales = CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date]))

Section: Page 5
Study and Interview Notes  |  Page 5
Q36. What are ALL, ALLEXCEPT and REMOVEFILTERS?
 Ans: They remove filters from a table or columns. Used for percentage of total calculations.
% of Total = DIVIDE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), ALL(Sales)))
Q37. Why use DIVIDE() instead of '/'?
 Ans: DIVIDE handles divide-by-zero safely, returning blank or an alternate result.
Q38. What is Row-Level Security (RLS)?
 Ans: Restricts data access per user using DAX filter rules on roles, e.g. [Region] = USERNAME().
Configured in Desktop, assigned in Service.
Visualisation and Performance
Q39. Which visual for which purpose?
 Ans: Trends: line chart. Comparison: bar/column. Part-to-whole: pie/donut/treemap. Relationship: scatter.
Single KPI: card/gauge. Geographic: map. Detail: table/matrix. Waterfall for variance.
Q40. What are Slicers, Drill-down and Drill-through?
 Ans: Slicers filter visuals interactively. Drill-down moves through a hierarchy within a visual. Drill-through
navigates to a detail page filtered by the selected item.
Q41. What are Bookmarks and Tooltips?
 Ans: Bookmarks save a report state (filters, visibility) for navigation/storytelling. Tooltips show extra

Section: Page 5
context
when hovering over a data point.
Q42. How do you optimise a slow Power BI report?
 Ans: Use star schema, remove unused columns/rows, prefer measures over calculated columns, reduce
cardinality, use Import mode, avoid bi-directional filters, use aggregations and Performance Analyzer / DAX
Studio.
Q43. What are Parameters and Incremental Refresh?
 Ans: Parameters make queries dynamic (e.g., file path). Incremental refresh refreshes only recent partitions
of large tables, saving time.
Q44. Common Power Query transformations?
 Ans: Remove duplicates, split/merge columns, pivot/unpivot, change types, replace values, append/merge
queries, group by, add custom/conditional columns.
Q45. Merge vs Append?
 Ans: Merge joins tables horizontally on keys (like SQL JOIN). Append stacks tables vertically (like UNION).

Section: Page 6
Study and Interview Notes  |  Page 6
3. Machine Learning
Basic Questions
Q46. What is Machine Learning?
 Ans: A subset of AI where algorithms learn patterns from data to make predictions or decisions without being
explicitly programmed.
Q47. Types of Machine Learning?
 Ans: Supervised (labelled data), Unsupervised (unlabelled), Semi-supervised, Reinforcement (agent learns
via rewards).
Q48. Classification vs Regression?
 Ans: Classification predicts discrete classes (spam/not spam). Regression predicts continuous values
(house price).
Q49. What is overfitting and underfitting?
 Ans: Overfitting: model learns noise, high train accuracy but poor test accuracy (high variance). Underfitting:
model too simple, poor on both (high bias).
Q50. How do you prevent overfitting?
 Ans: More data, cross-validation, regularisation (L1/L2), pruning, early stopping, dropout, feature selection,
ensemble methods.
Q51. Explain the Bias-Variance trade-off.
 Ans: Bias is error from overly simple assumptions; variance is sensitivity to training data fluctuations.
Reducing one usually increases the other; the goal is the optimal balance.
Q52. Train / Validation / Test split?
 Ans: Train fits the model,

Section: Page 6
validation tunes hyperparameters, test gives final unbiased performance estimate.
Common split 70/15/15 or 80/20.
Q53. What is cross-validation?
 Ans: Splitting data into k folds; train on k-1 and validate on the remaining, repeating k times and averaging
the score for robust evaluation.
Algorithms
Q54. How does Linear Regression work?
 Ans: Fits a line y = b0 + b1x1 + ... minimising sum of squared errors (OLS). Assumptions: linearity,
independence, homoscedasticity, normal residuals, no multicollinearity.
Q55. How does Logistic Regression work?
 Ans: Uses the sigmoid function to output probability of a class; trained by minimising log loss. Used for binary
classification.
Q56. How does a Decision Tree work?
 Ans: Recursively splits data on features that maximise information gain (entropy) or minimise Gini impurity,
forming a tree of decisions.
Q57. Random Forest vs Gradient Boosting?
 Ans: Random Forest: bagging, many independent trees averaged, reduces variance. Gradient Boosting
(XGBoost, LightGBM): trees built sequentially, each correcting previous errors, reduces bias.
Q58. Bagging vs Boosting?
 Ans: Bagging trains models in parallel on bootstrap samples. Boosting trains

Section: Page 6
sequentially, focusing on
previously misclassified samples.
Q59. How does KNN work?
 Ans: Classifies a point by majority vote (or averages) of its k nearest neighbours using a distance metric.
Lazy learner; needs feature scaling.

Section: Page 7
Study and Interview Notes  |  Page 7
Q60. What is SVM?
 Ans: Finds the hyperplane that maximises margin between classes. Kernel trick (RBF, polynomial) handles
non-linear data.
Q61. How does K-Means work?
 Ans: Choose k, initialise centroids, assign points to nearest centroid, recompute centroids, repeat until
convergence. Choose k with Elbow method / Silhouette score.
Q62. What is PCA?
 Ans: Dimensionality reduction that projects data onto orthogonal directions (principal components) capturing
maximum variance.
Q63. Naive Bayes - why 'naive'?
 Ans: Applies Bayes' theorem assuming features are conditionally independent given the class. Fast and
good for text classification.
Q64. L1 (Lasso) vs L2 (Ridge) regularisation?
 Ans: L1 adds absolute weights penalty and can shrink coefficients to zero (feature selection). L2 adds
squared weights penalty, shrinking coefficients smoothly.
Evaluation and Practical
Q65. What is a Confusion Matrix?
 Ans: Table of TP, FP, TN, FN used to compute metrics.
Q66. Define Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1.
 Ans: Accuracy = (TP+TN)/Total. Precision = TP/(TP+FP). Recall = TP/(TP+FN). F1 = 2*P*R/(P+R).
Q67. What is ROC-AUC?
 Ans: ROC plots True Positive

Section: Page 7
Rate vs False Positive Rate across thresholds; AUC is the area under it (1 =
perfect, 0.5 = random).
Q68. Regression metrics?
 Ans: MAE, MSE, RMSE, R-squared, Adjusted R-squared.
Q69. What is hyperparameter tuning?
 Ans: Selecting best model settings (e.g., depth, learning rate) via Grid Search, Random Search or Bayesian
optimisation.
Q70. What is data leakage?
 Ans: When information from outside the training set (e.g., test data or future info) influences training, giving
overly optimistic results.
Q71. Write a basic ML pipeline in scikit-learn.
 Ans: Split, scale, train, evaluate.
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=42)
sc = StandardScaler(); X_tr = sc.fit_transform(X_tr); X_te = sc.transform(X_te)
model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(classification_report(y_te, model.predict(X_te)))
Q72. Scenario: In fraud detection, which metric matters most?
 Ans: Recall (and precision / PR-AUC), because

Section: Page 7
missing fraud (false negatives) is costly and the data is
highly imbalanced; accuracy is misleading.

Section: Page 8
Study and Interview Notes  |  Page 8
4. Deep Learning
Basic Questions
Q73. What is Deep Learning?
 Ans: A subset of ML using multi-layer artificial neural networks to automatically learn hierarchical feature
representations from large data.
Q74. Deep Learning vs Machine Learning?
 Ans: DL learns features automatically, needs more data and compute (GPUs), and excels at
images/text/audio. Traditional ML needs manual feature engineering and works well on smaller tabular data.
Q75. What is a neuron / perceptron?
 Ans: Computes a weighted sum of inputs plus bias and passes it through an activation function: y = f(w.x +
b).
Q76. Common activation functions?
 Ans: Sigmoid (0-1), Tanh (-1 to 1), ReLU (max(0,x)), Leaky ReLU, Softmax (multi-class probabilities).
Q77. Why ReLU is preferred?
 Ans: It is cheap to compute, reduces vanishing gradient, and gives sparse activations. Drawback: dying
ReLU (fixed by Leaky ReLU/ELU).
Q78. What is a loss function?
 Ans: Measures prediction error. MSE for regression, Binary Cross-Entropy for binary classification,
Categorical Cross-Entropy for multi-class.
Training Concepts
Q79. Explain Forward and Backpropagation.
 Ans: Forward pass computes

Section: Page 8
predictions layer by layer. Backpropagation uses the chain rule to compute
gradients of loss with respect to weights, which are then updated.
Q80. What is Gradient Descent and its variants?
 Ans: Optimisation that updates weights opposite to the gradient. Batch (all data), Stochastic (one sample),
Mini-batch (small batches). Adaptive: Adam, RMSprop, AdaGrad.
Q81. What is learning rate?
 Ans: Step size of weight updates. Too high: divergence; too low: slow training. Use schedulers or adaptive
optimisers.
Q82. Vanishing and Exploding gradients?
 Ans: Gradients become extremely small or large in deep nets, stopping learning. Fix: ReLU, proper
initialisation (He/Xavier), batch norm, residual connections, gradient clipping, LSTM/GRU.
Q83. What is Dropout?
 Ans: Randomly deactivates neurons during training to prevent overfitting and co-adaptation.
Q84. What is Batch Normalization?
 Ans: Normalises layer inputs per mini-batch, stabilising and speeding up training and allowing higher
learning rates.
Q85. Epoch vs Batch vs Iteration?
 Ans: Epoch: one pass over the full dataset. Batch: samples per update. Iteration: one update step (iterations
per epoch = N / batch size).
Q86. What is Early

Section: Page 8
Stopping?
 Ans: Stop training when validation loss stops improving to avoid overfitting.
Architectures

Section: Page 9
Study and Interview Notes  |  Page 9
Q87. What is a CNN and its layers?
 Ans: Convolutional Neural Network for images: Convolution (feature extraction with filters), Activation
(ReLU), Pooling (downsampling), Flatten, Fully Connected, Softmax output.
Q88. What is padding and stride?
 Ans: Padding adds border pixels to preserve size; stride is the step of the filter. Output size = (N - F + 2P)/S
+ 1.
Q89. Famous CNN architectures?
 Ans: LeNet, AlexNet, VGG, ResNet (skip connections), Inception, MobileNet, EfficientNet.
Q90. What is an RNN and why LSTM?
 Ans: RNN processes sequences with hidden state memory but suffers vanishing gradients. LSTM uses
input, forget and output gates to retain long-term dependencies. GRU is a simpler variant.
Q91. What is the Transformer architecture?
 Ans: Uses self-attention instead of recurrence, processing all tokens in parallel; consists of encoder/decoder
with multi-head attention, positional encoding and feed-forward layers. Basis of BERT and GPT.
Q92. What is Transfer Learning?
 Ans: Reusing a pretrained model (e.g., ResNet, BERT) and fine-tuning it on a new task with less data.
Q93. What are Autoencoders and GANs?
 Ans: Autoencoder:

Section: Page 9
encoder-decoder that learns compressed representations (denoising, anomaly
detection). GAN: generator and discriminator compete to generate realistic data.
Q94. Write a simple Keras model.
 Ans: Binary classifier with dropout.
from tensorflow import keras
from tensorflow.keras import layers
model = keras.Sequential([
  layers.Dense(64, activation='relu', input_shape=(20,)),
  layers.Dropout(0.3),
  layers.Dense(32, activation='relu'),
  layers.Dense(1, activation='sigmoid')])
model.compile(optimizer='adam', loss='binary_crossentropy', metrics=['accuracy'])
model.fit(X_train, y_train, epochs=20, batch_size=32, validation_split=0.2)

Section: Page 10
Study and Interview Notes  |  Page 10
5. Artificial Intelligence (AI)
Basic Questions
Q95. What is Artificial Intelligence?
 Ans: The simulation of human intelligence in machines - reasoning, learning, perception, problem-solving
and language understanding.
Q96. AI vs ML vs DL vs Data Science?
 Ans: AI is the broad goal; ML is a subset that learns from data; DL is a subset of ML using deep neural
networks; Data Science uses these tools to extract insights from data.
Q97. Types of AI?
 Ans: By capability: Narrow (ANI), General (AGI), Super (ASI). By functionality: Reactive, Limited Memory,
Theory of Mind, Self-aware.
Q98. What are intelligent agents?
 Ans: Entities that perceive the environment via sensors and act via actuators to achieve goals. Types: simple
reflex, model-based, goal-based, utility-based, learning agents.
Q99. What is the Turing Test?
 Ans: A test proposed by Alan Turing: a machine is intelligent if a human cannot reliably distinguish its
responses from a human's.
Q100. Main applications of AI?
 Ans: Healthcare diagnosis, fraud detection, recommendation systems, self-driving cars, chatbots, computer
vision, speech recognition, robotics, predictive

Section: Page 10
maintenance.
Core Concepts
Q101. What is Natural Language Processing (NLP)?
 Ans: AI field enabling machines to understand and generate human language: tokenization,
stemming/lemmatization, POS tagging, NER, sentiment analysis, translation, summarisation.
Q102. What is Computer Vision?
 Ans: Enabling machines to interpret images/video: classification, object detection (YOLO), segmentation,
face recognition, OCR.
Q103. Uninformed vs Informed search?
 Ans: Uninformed: BFS, DFS, Uniform Cost (no domain knowledge). Informed: A*, Greedy Best-First using a
heuristic f(n) = g(n) + h(n).
Q104. What is a heuristic?
 Ans: A rule of thumb estimate of cost to goal that guides search to be more efficient.
Q105. What is Reinforcement Learning?
 Ans: An agent learns by interacting with an environment, receiving rewards or penalties. Key terms: agent,
environment, state, action, reward, policy. Example algorithms: Q-Learning, DQN, PPO.
Q106. What is an Expert System?
 Ans: AI system with a knowledge base and inference engine that mimics a human expert's decisions using
rules.
Q107. What is Knowledge Representation?
 Ans: Ways to store facts for reasoning: semantic networks, frames, ontologies,

Section: Page 10
propositional and first-order
logic.
Q108. What is a Recommendation System?
 Ans: Predicts user preferences. Content-based, Collaborative filtering (user/item based), and Hybrid
approaches.

Section: Page 11
Study and Interview Notes  |  Page 11
Ethics and Scenario
Q109. What is Explainable AI (XAI)?
 Ans: Techniques (SHAP, LIME, feature importance) that make model decisions understandable and
trustworthy.
Q110. What are the ethical concerns in AI?
 Ans: Bias and fairness, privacy, transparency, accountability, job displacement, misuse (deepfakes), and
security.
Q111. How can AI bias be reduced?
 Ans: Diverse and representative data, bias audits, fairness metrics, human oversight, explainability and
continuous monitoring.
Q112. Scenario: Design a customer-support chatbot.
 Ans: Define intents/use cases, collect conversations, use NLU/LLM with retrieval (RAG) over company
knowledge base, add fallback to human agent, evaluate with CSAT/resolution rate, and monitor for errors.

Section: Page 12
Study and Interview Notes  |  Page 12
6. Advanced AI
Generative AI and LLMs
Q113. What is Generative AI?
 Ans: AI that creates new content (text, images, code, audio, video) by learning data distributions. Examples:
GPT, Claude, Stable Diffusion, DALL-E.
Q114. What is a Large Language Model (LLM)?
 Ans: A transformer-based model with billions of parameters pretrained on massive text to predict the next
token; capable of generation, reasoning and summarisation.
Q115. Explain Self-Attention.
 Ans: Each token computes Query, Key and Value vectors; attention weights = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) are
used to weight values, letting the model focus on relevant tokens regardless of distance.
Q116. BERT vs GPT?
 Ans: BERT: encoder-only, bidirectional, masked language modelling, good for understanding tasks. GPT:
decoder-only, autoregressive, good for generation.
Q117. What are tokens and embeddings?
 Ans: Tokens are text units (words/subwords). Embeddings are dense vectors capturing semantic meaning;
similar meanings are close in vector space.
Q118. What is Prompt Engineering?
 Ans: Designing inputs to get better outputs: clear instructions, role, examples (few-shot),

Section: Page 12
chain-of-thought,
format constraints, and context.
Q119. What are Temperature and Top-p?
 Ans: Sampling controls. Higher temperature increases randomness/creativity; lower makes output
deterministic. Top-p limits sampling to the smallest set of tokens with cumulative probability p.
Q120. What are hallucinations and how to reduce them?
 Ans: Confident but incorrect or fabricated outputs. Reduce using RAG, grounding with sources, lower
temperature, verification, fine-tuning and guardrails.
Techniques and Architectures
Q121. What is RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)?
 Ans: Combines retrieval with generation: documents are chunked, embedded and stored in a vector
database; relevant chunks are retrieved for a query and passed to the LLM as context, giving up-to-date,
grounded answers.
Q122. Fine-tuning vs RAG vs Prompting?
 Ans: Prompting: cheapest, quick. RAG: injects external/current knowledge without training. Fine-tuning:
changes model behaviour/style/domain skills but needs data and compute.
Q123. What are LoRA and PEFT?
 Ans: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning methods. LoRA adds small low-rank trainable matrices to frozen
weights, drastically reducing memory and compute.
Q124.

Section: Page 12
What is RLHF?
 Ans: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: train a reward model from human preference rankings,
then optimise the LLM with RL (e.g., PPO) to align with human preferences.
Q125. What is a Vector Database?
 Ans: Stores embeddings and performs similarity search (cosine, dot product, ANN algorithms like HNSW).
Examples: Pinecone, FAISS, Chroma, Weaviate.

Section: Page 13
Study and Interview Notes  |  Page 13
Q126. What are AI Agents / Agentic AI?
 Ans: LLM-powered systems that plan, use tools (APIs, code, search), keep memory and take multi-step
actions to achieve goals autonomously. Patterns: ReAct, plan-and-execute, multi-agent systems.
Q127. What is Multimodal AI?
 Ans: Models that process and combine multiple data types (text, image, audio, video) in a single system.
Q128. What are Diffusion Models?
 Ans: Generative models that learn to reverse a gradual noising process, generating images by denoising
random noise step by step (Stable Diffusion).
Q129. What is Model Quantization / Distillation?
 Ans: Quantization reduces numeric precision (e.g., FP16 to INT8) to shrink models. Distillation trains a small
student model to mimic a large teacher.
Q130. What is the context window?
 Ans: The maximum number of tokens an LLM can consider (input + output) at once.
Responsible AI, MLOps and Scenarios
Q131. What is MLOps?
 Ans: Practices to deploy, monitor and maintain ML models in production: CI/CD, versioning, experiment
tracking (MLflow), monitoring, retraining pipelines, Docker/Kubernetes.
Q132. What is model drift?
 Ans: Degradation of performance

Section: Page 13
over time. Data drift: input distribution changes. Concept drift: relationship
between inputs and target changes. Monitor and retrain.
Q133. What are AI safety and alignment?
 Ans: Ensuring AI systems behave as intended and in line with human values: guardrails, red-teaming,
interpretability, content filtering and human oversight.
Q134. What is Federated Learning?
 Ans: Training models across decentralised devices without sharing raw data, preserving privacy.
Q135. What is Explainability for LLMs / Guardrails?
 Ans: Methods (attention analysis, citations, probing) and rules/filters ensuring outputs stay safe, accurate
and on-policy.
Q136. Scenario: Build a document Q&A system for a company.
 Ans: Ingest PDFs, chunk and embed them, store in vector DB, retrieve top-k chunks with hybrid search +
reranking, prompt LLM with context and citations, add access control, evaluate (faithfulness, relevance) and
monitor.
Q137. Scenario: LLM gives inconsistent answers in production. What do you do?
 Ans: Lower temperature, tighten prompt and output schema, add few-shot examples, use RAG for facts, add
validation/guardrails, log and evaluate with a test set, and consider fine-tuning.

1. Data Science
Basic Questions
Q1. What is Data Science?
 Ans: An interdisciplinary field that uses statistics, programming, domain knowledge and machine learning to
extract insights and build predictive solutions from structured and unstructured data.
Q2. Explain the Data Science lifecycle.
 Ans: 1) Problem definition 2) Data collection 3) Data cleaning 4) Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) 5) Feature
engineering 6) Model building 7) Evaluation 8) Deployment 9) Monitoring and maintenance.
Q3. Difference between Data Science, Data Analytics and Data Engineering?
 Ans: Data Science: predictive/prescriptive modelling. Data Analytics: descriptive analysis and reporting of
past data. Data Engineering: building pipelines, storage and infrastructure for data.
Q4. Structured vs Unstructured data?
 Ans: Structured: organised in rows/columns (SQL tables, CSV). Unstructured: no fixed schema (text,
images, audio, video). Semi-structured: JSON, XML.
Q5. What is Big Data? Mention the 5 Vs.
 Ans: Datasets too large/complex for traditional tools. Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, Value.
Q6. Population vs Sample?
 Ans: Population is the entire group of

Section: Page 2
interest; a sample is a subset used to draw inferences about the
population.
Q7. Which Python libraries are used in Data Science?
 Ans: NumPy, Pandas, Matplotlib, Seaborn, SciPy, Scikit-learn, Statsmodels, TensorFlow/PyTorch.
Statistics and Data Cleaning
Q8. Mean, Median, Mode - when to use each?
 Ans: Mean for symmetric data, median for skewed data or outliers, mode for categorical data.
Q9. What is standard deviation and variance?
 Ans: Variance is the average squared deviation from the mean; standard deviation is its square root and
shows spread in original units.
Q10. What is a p-value?
 Ans: The probability of observing results at least as extreme as the sample, assuming the null hypothesis is
true. If p < alpha (usually 0.05), reject the null hypothesis.
Q11. Type I vs Type II error?
 Ans: Type I: rejecting a true null (false positive). Type II: failing to reject a false null (false negative).
Q12. What is the Central Limit Theorem?
 Ans: The distribution of sample means approaches a normal distribution as sample size grows (n >= 30 is a
common rule), regardless of the population distribution.
Q13. Correlation vs Causation?
 Ans: Correlation shows two variables move

Section: Page 2
together; causation means one directly causes change in the
other. Correlation does not imply causation.
Q14. How do you handle missing values?
 Ans: Remove rows/columns, impute with mean/median/mode, forward/backward fill, KNN or model-based
imputation, or flag missingness as a feature.
Q15. How do you detect and handle outliers?
 Ans: Detect with IQR rule (below Q1-1.5*IQR or above Q3+1.5*IQR), Z-score (|z|>3), box plots. Handle by
removing, capping (winsorizing), transforming (log) or using robust models.

Section: Page 3
Study and Interview Notes  |  Page 3
Q16. Normalization vs Standardization?
 Ans: Normalization (Min-Max) scales to [0,1]. Standardization (Z-score) gives mean 0 and std 1. Use
standardization for algorithms assuming Gaussian data and distance-based models.
Q17. What is feature engineering?
 Ans: Creating, transforming or selecting variables (e.g., date parts, ratios, encodings, binning) to improve
model performance.
Q18. Label encoding vs One-hot encoding?
 Ans: Label encoding maps categories to integers (suitable for ordinal data). One-hot creates binary columns
per category (suitable for nominal data).
Scenario / Practical Questions
Q19. Your dataset is highly imbalanced (95% / 5%). What will you do?
 Ans: Use resampling (SMOTE oversampling, undersampling), class weights, appropriate metrics (Precision,
Recall, F1, PR-AUC instead of accuracy) and stratified cross-validation.
Q20. How would you explain a model to a non-technical stakeholder?
 Ans: Focus on business impact, use simple visuals, analogies and key drivers (feature importance, SHAP),
avoid jargon, and state limitations.

Basic Questions
Q22. What is Power BI?
 Ans: Microsoft's business intelligence tool for connecting to data, transforming, modelling and visualising it
through reports and dashboards.
Q23. Main components of Power BI?
 Ans: Power BI Desktop (authoring), Power BI Service (cloud sharing), Power BI Mobile, Power BI Report
Server, Power BI Gateway, Power Query and DAX.
Q24. Report vs Dashboard?
 Ans: A report is multi-page with many visuals built on one dataset. A dashboard is a single-page canvas of
pinned tiles from multiple reports.
Q25. What is Power Query?
 Ans: ETL tool (M language) used to connect, clean, transform and shape data before loading it into the
model.
Q26. What is DAX?
 Ans: Data Analysis Expressions - a formula language for calculated columns, measures and tables.
Q27. Import mode vs DirectQuery vs Live Connection?
 Ans: Import: data cached in memory, fastest. DirectQuery: queries source live, no data stored. Live
Connection: connects to SSAS/Power BI dataset; model lives externally. Composite models mix modes.
Q28. What is a Gateway?
 Ans: A bridge allowing Power BI Service to securely refresh

data from on-premises sources. Types:
On-premises (standard) and Personal mode.
Data Modelling and DAX
Q29. What is a Star Schema?
 Ans: A model with a central fact table (transactions) linked to dimension tables (customer, product, date). It is
the recommended modelling pattern for performance and simplicity.
Q30. Types of relationships in Power BI?
 Ans: One-to-many (most common), one-to-one, many-to-many. Cross-filter direction can be single or both.
Q31. Calculated column vs Measure?
 Ans: Calculated column: computed row by row at refresh, stored in memory, usable in slicers/rows. Measure:
computed at query time based on filter context, not stored, used for aggregations.
Q32. What is filter context and row context?
 Ans: Filter context is the set of filters (slicers, rows, columns, CALCULATE) applied to a calculation. Row
context iterates row by row (calculated columns, iterator functions like SUMX).
Q33. Explain CALCULATE().
 Ans: It evaluates an expression in a modified filter context.
Sales India = CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), Sales[Country] = "India")
Q34. SUM vs SUMX?
 Ans: SUM aggregates a single column. SUMX is an iterator that evaluates an expression row by row,

Section: Page 4
then
sums.
Total Revenue = SUMX(Sales, Sales[Qty] * Sales[Price])
Q35. Write a DAX for Year-to-Date and Previous Year sales.
 Ans: Requires a proper Date table marked as Date Table.
YTD Sales = TOTALYTD(SUM(Sales[Amount]), 'Date'[Date])
PY Sales = CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date]))

Q36. What are ALL, ALLEXCEPT and REMOVEFILTERS?
 Ans: They remove filters from a table or columns. Used for percentage of total calculations.
% of Total = DIVIDE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), ALL(Sales)))
Q37. Why use DIVIDE() instead of '/'?
 Ans: DIVIDE handles divide-by-zero safely, returning blank or an alternate result.
Q38. What is Row-Level Security (RLS)?
 Ans: Restricts data access per user using DAX filter rules on roles, e.g. [Region] = USERNAME().
Configured in Desktop, assigned in Service.

Q39. Which visual for which purpose?
 Ans: Trends: line chart. Comparison: bar/column. Part-to-whole: pie/donut/treemap. Relationship: scatter.
Single KPI: card/gauge. Geographic: map. Detail: table/matrix. Waterfall for variance.
Q40. What are Slicers, Drill-down and Drill-through?
 Ans: Slicers filter visuals interactively. Drill-down moves through a hierarchy within a visual. Drill-through
navigates to a detail page filtered by the selected item.
Q41. What are Bookmarks and Tooltips?
 Ans: Bookmarks save a report state (filters, visibility) for navigation/storytelling. Tooltips show extra

context
when hovering over a data point.

cardinality, use Import mode, avoid bi-directional filters, use aggregations and Performance Analyzer / DAX
Studio.
Q43. What are Parameters and Incremental Refresh?
 Ans: Parameters make queries dynamic (e.g., file path). Incremental refresh refreshes only recent partitions
of large tables, saving time.
Q44. Common Power Query transformations?
 Ans: Remove duplicates, split/merge columns, pivot/unpivot, change types, replace values, append/merge
queries, group by, add custom/conditional columns.
Q45. Merge vs Append?
 Ans: Merge joins tables horizontally on keys (like SQL JOIN). Append stacks tables vertically (like UNION).

3. Machine Learning
Basic Questions
Q46. What is Machine Learning?
 Ans: A subset of AI where algorithms learn patterns from data to make predictions or decisions without being
explicitly programmed.
Q47. Types of Machine Learning?
 Ans: Supervised (labelled data), Unsupervised (unlabelled), Semi-supervised, Reinforcement (agent learns
via rewards).
Q48. Classification vs Regression?
 Ans: Classification predicts discrete classes (spam/not spam). Regression predicts continuous values
(house price).
Q49. What is overfitting and underfitting?
 Ans: Overfitting: model learns noise, high train accuracy but poor test accuracy (high variance). Underfitting:
model too simple, poor on both (high bias).
Q50. How do you prevent overfitting?
 Ans: More data, cross-validation, regularisation (L1/L2), pruning, early stopping, dropout, feature selection,
ensemble methods.
Q51. Explain the Bias-Variance trade-off.
 Ans: Bias is error from overly simple assumptions; variance is sensitivity to training data fluctuations.
Reducing one usually increases the other; the goal is the optimal balance.
Q52. Train / Validation / Test split?
 Ans: Train fits the model,

Section: Page 6
validation tunes hyperparameters, test gives final unbiased performance estimate.
Common split 70/15/15 or 80/20.
Q53. What is cross-validation?
 Ans: Splitting data into k folds; train on k-1 and validate on the remaining, repeating k times and averaging
the score for robust evaluation.
Algorithms
Q54. How does Linear Regression work?
 Ans: Fits a line y = b0 + b1x1 + ... minimising sum of squared errors (OLS). Assumptions: linearity,
independence, homoscedasticity, normal residuals, no multicollinearity.
Q55. How does Logistic Regression work?
 Ans: Uses the sigmoid function to output probability of a class; trained by minimising log loss. Used for binary
classification.
Q56. How does a Decision Tree work?
 Ans: Recursively splits data on features that maximise information gain (entropy) or minimise Gini impurity,
forming a tree of decisions.
Q57. Random Forest vs Gradient Boosting?
 Ans: Random Forest: bagging, many independent trees averaged, reduces variance. Gradient Boosting
(XGBoost, LightGBM): trees built sequentially, each correcting previous errors, reduces bias.
Q58. Bagging vs Boosting?
 Ans: Bagging trains models in parallel on bootstrap samples. Boosting trains

Section: Page 6
sequentially, focusing on
previously misclassified samples.
Q59. How does KNN work?
 Ans: Classifies a point by majority vote (or averages) of its k nearest neighbours using a distance metric.
Lazy learner; needs feature scaling.

Section: Page 7
Study and Interview Notes  |  Page 7
Q60. What is SVM?
 Ans: Finds the hyperplane that maximises margin between classes. Kernel trick (RBF, polynomial) handles
non-linear data.
Q61. How does K-Means work?
 Ans: Choose k, initialise centroids, assign points to nearest centroid, recompute centroids, repeat until
convergence. Choose k with Elbow method / Silhouette score.
Q62. What is PCA?
 Ans: Dimensionality reduction that projects data onto orthogonal directions (principal components) capturing
maximum variance.
Q63. Naive Bayes - why 'naive'?
 Ans: Applies Bayes' theorem assuming features are conditionally independent given the class. Fast and
good for text classification.
Q64. L1 (Lasso) vs L2 (Ridge) regularisation?
 Ans: L1 adds absolute weights penalty and can shrink coefficients to zero (feature selection). L2 adds
squared weights penalty, shrinking coefficients smoothly.
Evaluation and Practical
Q65. What is a Confusion Matrix?
 Ans: Table of TP, FP, TN, FN used to compute metrics.
Q66. Define Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1.
 Ans: Accuracy = (TP+TN)/Total. Precision = TP/(TP+FP). Recall = TP/(TP+FN). F1 = 2*P*R/(P+R).
Q67. What is ROC-AUC?
 Ans: ROC plots True Positive

Section: Page 7
Rate vs False Positive Rate across thresholds; AUC is the area under it (1 =
perfect, 0.5 = random).
Q68. Regression metrics?
 Ans: MAE, MSE, RMSE, R-squared, Adjusted R-squared.
Q69. What is hyperparameter tuning?
 Ans: Selecting best model settings (e.g., depth, learning rate) via Grid Search, Random Search or Bayesian
optimisation.
Q70. What is data leakage?
 Ans: When information from outside the training set (e.g., test data or future info) influences training, giving
overly optimistic results.
Q71. Write a basic ML pipeline in scikit-learn.

4. Deep Learning
Basic Questions
Q73. What is Deep Learning?
 Ans: A subset of ML using multi-layer artificial neural networks to automatically learn hierarchical feature
representations from large data.
Q74. Deep Learning vs Machine Learning?
 Ans: DL learns features automatically, needs more data and compute (GPUs), and excels at
images/text/audio. Traditional ML needs manual feature engineering and works well on smaller tabular data.
Q75. What is a neuron / perceptron?
 Ans: Computes a weighted sum of inputs plus bias and passes it through an activation function: y = f(w.x +
b).
Q76. Common activation functions?
 Ans: Sigmoid (0-1), Tanh (-1 to 1), ReLU (max(0,x)), Leaky ReLU, Softmax (multi-class probabilities).
Q77. Why ReLU is preferred?
 Ans: It is cheap to compute, reduces vanishing gradient, and gives sparse activations. Drawback: dying
ReLU (fixed by Leaky ReLU/ELU).
Q78. What is a loss function?
 Ans: Measures prediction error. MSE for regression, Binary Cross-Entropy for binary classification,
Categorical Cross-Entropy for multi-class.
Training Concepts
Q79. Explain Forward and Backpropagation.
 Ans: Forward pass computes

Section: Page 8
predictions layer by layer. Backpropagation uses the chain rule to compute
gradients of loss with respect to weights, which are then updated.
Q80. What is Gradient Descent and its variants?
 Ans: Optimisation that updates weights opposite to the gradient. Batch (all data), Stochastic (one sample),
Mini-batch (small batches). Adaptive: Adam, RMSprop, AdaGrad.
Q81. What is learning rate?
 Ans: Step size of weight updates. Too high: divergence; too low: slow training. Use schedulers or adaptive
optimisers.
Q82. Vanishing and Exploding gradients?
 Ans: Gradients become extremely small or large in deep nets, stopping learning. Fix: ReLU, proper
initialisation (He/Xavier), batch norm, residual connections, gradient clipping, LSTM/GRU.
Q83. What is Dropout?
 Ans: Randomly deactivates neurons during training to prevent overfitting and co-adaptation.
Q84. What is Batch Normalization?
 Ans: Normalises layer inputs per mini-batch, stabilising and speeding up training and allowing higher
learning rates.
Q85. Epoch vs Batch vs Iteration?
 Ans: Epoch: one pass over the full dataset. Batch: samples per update. Iteration: one update step (iterations
per epoch = N / batch size).
Q86. What is Early

Section: Page 8
Stopping?
 Ans: Stop training when validation loss stops improving to avoid overfitting.
Architectures

Q87. What is a CNN and its layers?
 Ans: Convolutional Neural Network for images: Convolution (feature extraction with filters), Activation
(ReLU), Pooling (downsampling), Flatten, Fully Connected, Softmax output.
Q88. What is padding and stride?
 Ans: Padding adds border pixels to preserve size; stride is the step of the filter. Output size = (N - F + 2P)/S
+ 1.
Q89. Famous CNN architectures?
 Ans: LeNet, AlexNet, VGG, ResNet (skip connections), Inception, MobileNet, EfficientNet.
Q90. What is an RNN and why LSTM?
 Ans: RNN processes sequences with hidden state memory but suffers vanishing gradients. LSTM uses
input, forget and output gates to retain long-term dependencies. GRU is a simpler variant.
Q91. What is the Transformer architecture?
 Ans: Uses self-attention instead of recurrence, processing all tokens in parallel; consists of encoder/decoder
with multi-head attention, positional encoding and feed-forward layers. Basis of BERT and GPT.
Q92. What is Transfer Learning?
 Ans: Reusing a pretrained model (e.g., ResNet, BERT) and fine-tuning it on a new task with less data.
Q93. What are Autoencoders and GANs?
 Ans: Autoencoder:

Section: Page 9
encoder-decoder that learns compressed representations (denoising, anomaly
detection). GAN: generator and discriminator compete to generate realistic data.

Basic Questions

 Ans: The simulation of human intelligence in machines - reasoning, learning, perception, problem-solving

 Ans: AI is the broad goal; ML is a subset that learns from data; DL is a subset of ML using deep neural

 Ans: A test proposed by Alan Turing: a machine is intelligent if a human cannot reliably distinguish its

 Ans: A rule of thumb estimate of cost to goal that guides search to be more efficient.

 Ans: AI system with a knowledge base and inference engine that mimics a human expert's decisions using

 Ans: Ways to store facts for reasoning: semantic networks, frames, ontologies,

propositional and first-order
logic.

 Ans: Techniques (SHAP, LIME, feature importance) that make model decisions understandable and

Generative AI and LLMs
Q113. What is Generative AI?
 Ans: AI that creates new content (text, images, code, audio, video) by learning data distributions. Examples:
GPT, Claude, Stable Diffusion, DALL-E.
Q114. What is a Large Language Model (LLM)?
 Ans: A transformer-based model with billions of parameters pretrained on massive text to predict the next
token; capable of generation, reasoning and summarisation.
Q115. Explain Self-Attention.
 Ans: Each token computes Query, Key and Value vectors; attention weights = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) are
used to weight values, letting the model focus on relevant tokens regardless of distance.
Q116. BERT vs GPT?
 Ans: BERT: encoder-only, bidirectional, masked language modelling, good for understanding tasks. GPT:
decoder-only, autoregressive, good for generation.
Q117. What are tokens and embeddings?
 Ans: Tokens are text units (words/subwords). Embeddings are dense vectors capturing semantic meaning;
similar meanings are close in vector space.
Q118. What is Prompt Engineering?
 Ans: Designing inputs to get better outputs: clear instructions, role, examples (few-shot),

chain-of-thought,
format constraints, and context.
Q119. What are Temperature and Top-p?
 Ans: Sampling controls. Higher temperature increases randomness/creativity; lower makes output
deterministic. Top-p limits sampling to the smallest set of tokens with cumulative probability p.
Q120. What are hallucinations and how to reduce them?
 Ans: Confident but incorrect or fabricated outputs. Reduce using RAG, grounding with sources, lower
temperature, verification, fine-tuning and guardrails.
Techniques and Architectures
Q121. What is RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)?
 Ans: Combines retrieval with generation: documents are chunked, embedded and stored in a vector
database; relevant chunks are retrieved for a query and passed to the LLM as context, giving up-to-date,
grounded answers.
Q122. Fine-tuning vs RAG vs Prompting?
 Ans: Prompting: cheapest, quick. RAG: injects external/current knowledge without training. Fine-tuning:
changes model behaviour/style/domain skills but needs data and compute.
Q123. What are LoRA and PEFT?
 Ans: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning methods. LoRA adds small low-rank trainable matrices to frozen
weights, drastically reducing memory and compute.
Q124.

What is RLHF?
 Ans: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: train a reward model from human preference rankings,
then optimise the LLM with RL (e.g., PPO) to align with human preferences.
Q125. What is a Vector Database?
 Ans: Stores embeddings and performs similarity search (cosine, dot product, ANN algorithms like HNSW).
Examples: Pinecone, FAISS, Chroma, Weaviate.

Q126. What are AI Agents / Agentic AI?

Q127. What is Multimodal AI?
 Ans: Models that process and combine multiple data types (text, image, audio, video) in a single system.
Q128. What are Diffusion Models?
 Ans: Generative models that learn to reverse a gradual noising process, generating images by denoising
random noise step by step (Stable Diffusion).
Q129. What is Model Quantization / Distillation?
 Ans: Quantization reduces numeric precision (e.g., FP16 to INT8) to shrink models. Distillation trains a small
student model to mimic a large teacher.
Q130. What is the context window?
 Ans: The maximum number of tokens an LLM can consider (input + output) at once.
Responsible AI, MLOps and Scenarios
Q131. What is MLOps?
 Ans: Practices to deploy, monitor and maintain ML models in production: CI/CD, versioning, experiment
tracking (MLflow), monitoring, retraining pipelines, Docker/Kubernetes.
Q132. What is model drift?
 Ans: Degradation of performance

Q133. What are AI safety and alignment?
 Ans: Ensuring AI systems behave as intended and in line with human values: guardrails, red-teaming,

Q134. What is Federated Learning?
 Ans: Training models across decentralised devices without sharing raw data, preserving privacy.

 Ans: Ingest PDFs, chunk and embed them, store in vector DB, retrieve top-k chunks with hybrid search +

Q137. Scenario: LLM gives inconsistent answers in production. What do you do?
 Ans: Lower temperature, tighten prompt and output schema, add few-shot examples, use RAG for facts, add
